newsitem.title: GERMANY: German troops battle to mend damaged Oder dike.
newsitem.headline: German troops battle to mend damaged Oder dike.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers worked furiously on Thursday to prevent a damaged dike on the River Oder from bursting open and unleashing a catastrophic flood.

Helicopters were dumping five-ton sacks of sand at the foot of the dike near Hohenwutzen to reinforce two areas where its foundations had cracked under the weight of two weeks of floods, threatening to burst completely.

Should the dike break, local officials said a wall of water several metres high would begin rushing into the fertile Oderbruch basin, filling a 250 square km area within hours until coming up against a wall of secondary dikes.

Nearly two dozen villages would initially be engulfed and, if the second line of dikes failed, the tide could flow southward through the rest of the Oderbruch valley some 17 km (11 miles) to the larger towns of Wriezen and Bad Freienwalde.

Some of the worst floods this century have hit neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

Around 10,000 residents of the Oder valley region on Germany's border with Poland were evacuated late on Wednesday, after the dike at Hohenwutzen threatened to give way. About 5,000 people were evacuated from the region last week.
Alvin Ziel, Brandenburg state interior minister, said the water was expected to rise slightly later in the day, around two to three cm, prolonging the pressure on the weakened dikes.

"We are on maximum alert. The chances of beating the sheer force of nature at this area (of the dike) are no higher than 10 to 15 percent," Ziel told ZDF television. "The situation is not getting better, but rather more critical day by day," he said.
The Oderbruch region, once the bread basket of communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago by King Frederick the Great of Prussia to create fertile farmland out of the Oderbruch, or Oder swamp.

The last time the dike broke was in 1947, near Reitwein, at the southern end of the Oderbruch. This time the weak point is near Hohenwutzen, where a sharp westward bend in the river is causing the water to press against the dikes.

Soldiers, aid workers and villagers have been trying to reinforce the sagging barriers for over a week near Hohenwutzen. The dikes have already broken further south, submerging over 100 homes in Wiesenau and Ziltendorf.

The flood crisis committee set up by Brandenburg state said a 15 metre tear in the foundation of the Hohenwutzen dike running parallel to the top of the dike appeared overnight just 100 metres south of a gap that opened up on Wednesday.

Steady flood levels and heavy rains made matters worse, where 5,000 soldiers were toiling to patch the dike and prevent a total break. Soldiers had to be removed from the dike periodically whenever the danger of it bursting became acute.

As light began to break over the line of trees in Poland on the eastern shore of the swollen river, soldiers who had worked all night were replaced with fresh troops. Some were so exhausted they laid down immediately and went to sleep on the muddy edge of the dike without blankets or shelter.
"We've been on our feet for 36 hours, some even for 49 hours," said navy seaman Holk Schilling, who was on the dike when it collapsed during the night.
"I could feel my heart drop into my stomach when the ground slipped out from under my feet."
Army captain Michael Schierenberg fixed his red beret and looked out over the swollen river. "It would be a miracle if the dike held -- but why shouldn't miracles happen?"
